function.name: glob_files
function.description: Recursively list workspace-relative file paths that match a glob, in sorted order. The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. It never matches file contents. Cache and VCS directories (.git, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, .venv, node_modules) are skipped.

path.description: Directory (or single file) to list under, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with 1-based line numbers. start_line and end_line are inclusive; omit start_line to begin at line 1 and end_line to read to the end. The header reports the range returned and the file's total lines. Long results are shown partially with an output id for paging.

function.name: outline
function.description: List the classes and functions of a Python file with line numbers.

function.name: search_text
function.description: Search file contents for exact text (literal characters, case-sensitive; not a regex). Returns one line per match as path:line: text, with 1-based line numbers, and states the scope searched. file_glob only selects which files are searched.

query.description: Required. The exact text to find, e.g. 'def get_real_name('.

path.description: File or directory to search, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

file_glob.description: Optional glob selecting files by relative path or file name (same rules as glob_files), e.g. '*.py'. It never matches file contents. Default '*'.

function.name: replace_text
function.description: Replace exact text in a file. Fails without changing the file if old_text is absent, or if it occurs more than once while replace_all is false; set replace_all to replace every occurrence. Reports how many occurrences were replaced and shows the edited lines.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Create a file, or overwrite it completely if it already exists, with the given content. Missing parent directories are created. Paths are relative to the workspace root.

function.name: run
function.description: Run one command in the workspace root without a shell: no pipes, redirection, chaining (&&, ;), cd, or variable expansion; use workspace-relative paths with forward slashes. 'python' and 'pytest' use the task's Python environment. Shows the command, status (including timeout), exit code, stdout, and stderr; long output is shown partially with an output id for paging. A successful exit does not mean the task is accepted.

function.name: read_output
function.description: Read part of an earlier tool result by its output id (for example out_12). Results that were shown partially say which id and range to request. Give start_line/end_line, or start_byte/end_byte for very long lines.

function.name: search_output
function.description: Find lines containing a literal string (plain text, not a regex) in an earlier tool result by its output id.

query.description: Required. The literal text to find.

function.name: history
function.description: Page through authorized durable session history. The response includes a stable next_cursor.

function.name: search_history
function.description: Find literal text in authorized prior actions and observations without knowing an output ID.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read an authorized session artifact by ID, optionally using an exact byte range.

function.name: note
function.description: Save a named plain-text note that persists across turns. Pinned notes are placed in context when space allows.

function.name: read_note
function.description: Read a saved note by name.

function.name: finish
function.description: Declare the work complete. The final workspace is then checked independently.

    1| # AGENTS.md

    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)

   30| ## Architecture
   31|

   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.

  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.

function.name: glob_files
function.description: Recursively list workspace-relative file paths that match a glob, in sorted order. The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. It never matches file contents. Cache and VCS directories (.git, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, .venv, node_modules) are skipped.

path.description: Directory (or single file) to list under, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with 1-based line numbers. start_line and end_line are inclusive; omit start_line to begin at line 1 and end_line to read to the end. The header reports the range returned and the file's total lines. Long results are shown partially with an output id for paging.

function.name: outline
function.description: List the classes and functions of a Python file with line numbers.

function.name: search_text
function.description: Search file contents for exact text (literal characters, case-sensitive; not a regex). Returns one line per match as path:line: text, with 1-based line numbers, and states the scope searched. file_glob only selects which files are searched.

query.description: Required. The exact text to find, e.g. 'def get_real_name('.

path.description: File or directory to search, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

file_glob.description: Optional glob selecting files by relative path or file name (same rules as glob_files), e.g. '*.py'. It never matches file contents. Default '*'.

function.name: replace_text
function.description: Replace exact text in a file. Fails without changing the file if old_text is absent, or if it occurs more than once while replace_all is false; set replace_all to replace every occurrence. Reports how many occurrences were replaced and shows the edited lines.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Create a file, or overwrite it completely if it already exists, with the given content. Missing parent directories are created. Paths are relative to the workspace root.

function.name: run
function.description: Run one command in the workspace root without a shell: no pipes, redirection, chaining (&&, ;), cd, or variable expansion; use workspace-relative paths with forward slashes. 'python' and 'pytest' use the task's Python environment. Shows the command, status (including timeout), exit code, stdout, and stderr; long output is shown partially with an output id for paging. A successful exit does not mean the task is accepted.

function.name: read_output
function.description: Read part of an earlier tool result by its output id (for example out_12). Results that were shown partially say which id and range to request. Give start_line/end_line, or start_byte/end_byte for very long lines.

function.name: search_output
function.description: Find lines containing a literal string (plain text, not a regex) in an earlier tool result by its output id.

query.description: Required. The literal text to find.

function.name: history
function.description: Page through authorized durable session history. The response includes a stable next_cursor.

function.name: search_history
function.description: Find literal text in authorized prior actions and observations without knowing an output ID.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read an authorized session artifact by ID, optionally using an exact byte range.

function.name: note
function.description: Save a named plain-text note that persists across turns. Pinned notes are placed in context when space allows.

function.name: read_note
function.description: Read a saved note by name.

function.name: finish
function.description: Declare the work complete. The final workspace is then checked independently.

    1| # AGENTS.md
    2| 
    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)
   29| 
   30| ## Architecture
   31| 
   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.
  110| 
  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.
  113| 
  114| ## Testing Conventions
  115| 
  116| - Tests are in `tests/` directory
  117| - Test files follow pattern `test_*.py`
  118| - Uses pytest framework
  119| - Test data often includes SQL strings with expected parsing/formatting results

    1| # AGENTS.md

    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)

   30| ## Architecture

   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:

   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.

   63|

   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets

   74|

   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping

   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:

  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)

    1| # AGENTS.md
    2| 
    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)
   29| 
   30| ## Architecture
   31| 
   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.
  110| 
  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.
  113| 
  114| ## Testing Conventions
  115| 
  116| - Tests are in `tests/` directory
  117| - Test files follow pattern `test_*.py`
  118| - Uses pytest framework
  119| - Test data often includes SQL strings with expected parsing/formatting results

    1| # AGENTS.md
    2| 
    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)
   29| 
   30| ## Architecture
   31| 
   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.
  110| 
  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.
  113| 
  114| ## Testing Conventions
  115| 
  116| - Tests are in `tests/` directory
  117| - Test files follow pattern `test_*.py`
  118| - Uses pytest framework
  119| - Test data often includes SQL strings with expected parsing/formatting results

    1| # AGENTS.md
    2| 
    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)
   29| 
   30| ## Architecture
   31| 
   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.
  110| 
  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.
  113|

  116| - Tests are in `tests/` directory
  117| - Test files follow pattern `test_*.py`
  118| - Uses pytest framework
  119| - Test data often includes SQL strings with expected parsing/formatting results

The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. {"content":"Found and fixed the regression. In `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`, the `post()` callback inside `group_period()` had its conditional branches swapped: when the next token was a valid extension (e.g. a wildcard `*`, function, or bracketed name after a `.`), it was returning `(pidx, tidx)` (stopping at the period) instead of `(pidx, nidx)` (extending through the next token) — and vice versa. This caused constructs like `a.*` in identifier lists to be grouped incorrectly, breaking downstream identifier-list detection and reindent formatting (e.g. `select a.*, b.c from a, b` no longer reindented correctly), as well as JSON-operator and wildcard grouping tests.

Fix applied:
```python
return (pidx, nidx) if valid_next else (pidx, tidx)
```
(previously `return (pidx, tidx) if valid_next else (pidx, nidx)`).

Verified manually with several cases (`select a.*, b.c from a, b`, `select a.* from a, b`, `select a.b[1] from foo`, JSON `->`/`->>` operators, plain identifier lists) — all now produce correct grouped output and correct reindented formatting. The `tests/` directory isn't present in this sandboxed checkout, so I validated behavior via direct `sqlparse.format`/`sqlparse.parse` calls instead of the hidden test suite, but the fix directly targets the described regression (wildcard/period grouping affecting reindent, json ops, and identifier-list grouping).","tool_calls":[]}

message.content:
Found and fixed the regression. In `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`, the `post()` callback inside `group_period()` had its conditional branches swapped: when the next token was a valid extension (e.g. a wildcard `*`, function, or bracketed name after a `.`), it was returning `(pidx, tidx)` (stopping at the period) instead of `(pidx, nidx)` (extending through the next token) — and vice versa. This caused constructs like `a.*` in identifier lists to be grouped incorrectly, breaking downstream identifier-list detection and reindent formatting (e.g. `select a.*, b.c from a, b` no longer reindented correctly), as well as JSON-operator and wildcard grouping tests.

Fix applied:
```python
return (pidx, nidx) if valid_next else (pidx, tidx)
```
(previously `return (pidx, tidx) if valid_next else (pidx, nidx)`).

Verified manually with several cases (`select a.*, b.c from a, b`, `select a.* from a, b`, `select a.b[1] from foo`, JSON `->`/`->>` operators, plain identifier lists) — all now produce correct grouped output and correct reindented formatting. The `tests/` directory isn't present in this sandboxed checkout, so I validated behavior via direct `sqlparse.format`/`sqlparse.parse` calls instead of the hidden test suite, but the fix directly targets the described regression (wildcard/period grouping affecting reindent, json ops, and identifier-list grouping).

    1| # AGENTS.md
    2| 
    3| This file provides guidance to Agents when working with code in this repository.
    4| 
    5| ## Project Overview
    6| 
    7| sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python that provides support for parsing, splitting, and formatting SQL statements. It's compatible with Python 3.10+ and supports multiple SQL dialects (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL/PL/pgSQL, HQL, MS Access, Snowflake, BigQuery).
    8| 
    9| ## Development Commands
   10| 
   11| This project uses `uv` for dependency and environment management. Common commands:
   12| 
   13| ### Testing
   14| - Run all tests across Python versions: `make test`
   15| - Run tests for specific Python version: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/`
   16| - Run single test file: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py`
   17| - Run specific test: `uv run --group dev --python 3.11 pytest tests/test_format.py::test_name`
   18| - Using Makefile: `make test`
   19| 
   20| ### Linting
   21| - `uv run --group dev ruff check sqlparse/` or `make lint`
   22| 
   23| ### Coverage
   24| - `make coverage` (runs tests with coverage and shows report)
   25| - `make coverage-xml` (generates XML coverage report)
   26| 
   27| ### Building
   28| - `python -m build` (builds distribution packages)
   29| 
   30| ## Architecture
   31| 
   32| ### Core Processing Pipeline
   33| 
   34| The parsing and formatting workflow follows this sequence:
   35| 
   36| 1. **Lexing** (`sqlparse/lexer.py`): Tokenizes SQL text into `(token_type, value)` pairs using regex-based pattern matching
   37| 2. **Filtering** (`sqlparse/engine/filter_stack.py`): Processes token stream through a `FilterStack` with three stages:
   38|    - `preprocess`: Token-level filters
   39|    - `stmtprocess`: Statement-level filters
   40|    - `postprocess`: Final output filters
   41| 3. **Statement Splitting** (`sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`): Splits token stream into individual SQL statements
   42| 4. **Grouping** (`sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`): Groups tokens into higher-level syntactic structures (parentheses, functions, identifiers, etc.)
   43| 5. **Formatting** (`sqlparse/formatter.py` + `sqlparse/filters/`): Applies formatting filters based on options
   44| 
   45| ### Token Hierarchy
   46| 
   47| The token system is defined in `sqlparse/sql.py`:
   48| 
   49| - `Token`: Base class with `value`, `ttype` (token type), and `parent` attributes
   50| - `TokenList`: Group of tokens, base for all syntactic structures
   51|   - `Statement`: Top-level SQL statement
   52|   - `Identifier`: Table/column names, possibly with aliases
   53|   - `IdentifierList`: Comma-separated identifiers
   54|   - `Function`: Function calls with parameters
   55|   - `Parenthesis`, `SquareBrackets`: Bracketed expressions
   56|   - `Case`, `If`, `For`, `Begin`: Control structures
   57|   - `Where`, `Having`, `Over`: SQL clauses
   58|   - `Comparison`, `Operation`: Expressions
   59| 
   60| All tokens maintain parent-child relationships for tree traversal.
   61| 
   62| ### Token Types
   63| 
   64| Token types are defined in `sqlparse/tokens.py` and used for classification during lexing (e.g., `T.Keyword.DML`, `T.Name`, `T.Punctuation`).
   65| 
   66| ### Keywords and Lexer Configuration
   67| 
   68| `sqlparse/keywords.py` contains:
   69| - `SQL_REGEX`: List of regex patterns for tokenization
   70| - Multiple `KEYWORDS_*` dictionaries for different SQL dialects
   71| - The `Lexer` class uses a singleton pattern (`Lexer.get_default_instance()`) that can be configured with different keyword sets
   72| 
   73| ### Grouping Algorithm
   74| 
   75| `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py` contains the grouping logic that transforms flat token lists into nested tree structures. Key functions:
   76| 
   77| - `_group_matching()`: Groups tokens with matching open/close markers (parentheses, CASE/END, etc.)
   78| - Various `group_*()` functions for specific constructs (identifiers, functions, comparisons, etc.)
   79| - Includes DoS protection via `MAX_GROUPING_DEPTH` and `MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS` limits
   80| 
   81| ### Formatting Filters
   82| 
   83| `sqlparse/filters/` contains various formatting filters:
   84| - `reindent.py`: Indentation logic
   85| - `aligned_indent.py`: Aligned indentation style
   86| - `right_margin.py`: Line wrapping
   87| - `tokens.py`: Token-level transformations (keyword case, etc.)
   88| - `output.py`: Output format serialization (SQL, Python, PHP)
   89| - `others.py`: Miscellaneous filters (strip comments, whitespace, etc.)
   90| 
   91| ## Public API
   92| 
   93| The main entry points in `sqlparse/__init__.py`:
   94| 
   95| - `parse(sql, encoding=None)`: Parse SQL into tuple of `Statement` objects
   96| - `format(sql, encoding=None, **options)`: Format SQL with options (reindent, keyword_case, etc.)
   97| - `split(sql, encoding=None, strip_semicolon=False)`: Split SQL into individual statement strings
   98| - `parsestream(stream, encoding=None)`: Generator version of parse for file-like objects
   99| 
  100| ## Important Patterns
  101| 
  102| ### Token Traversal
  103| - `token.flatten()`: Recursively yields all leaf tokens (ungrouped)
  104| - `token_first()`, `token_next()`, `token_prev()`: Navigate token lists
  105| - `token_next_by(i=, m=, t=)`: Find next token by instance type, match criteria, or token type
  106| - `token.match(ttype, values, regex=False)`: Check if token matches criteria
  107| 
  108| ### Adding Keyword Support
  109| Use `Lexer.add_keywords()` to extend the parser with new keywords for different SQL dialects.
  110| 
  111| ### DoS Prevention
  112| Be aware of recursion limits and token count limits in grouping operations when handling untrusted SQL input.
  113| 
  114| ## Testing Conventions
  115| 
  116| - Tests are in `tests/` directory
  117| - Test files follow pattern `test_*.py`
  118| - Uses pytest framework
  119| - Test data often includes SQL strings with expected parsing/formatting results

Found and fixed the regression. In `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`, the `post()` callback inside `group_period()` had its conditional branches swapped: when the next token was a valid extension (e.g. a wildcard `*`, function, or bracketed name after a `.`), it was returning `(pidx, tidx)` (stopping at the period) instead of `(pidx, nidx)` (extending through the next token) — and vice versa. This caused constructs like `a.*` in identifier lists to be grouped incorrectly, breaking downstream identifier-list detection and reindent formatting (e.g. `select a.*, b.c from a, b` no longer reindented correctly), as well as JSON-operator and wildcard grouping tests.

Fix applied:
```python
return (pidx, nidx) if valid_next else (pidx, tidx)
```
(previously `return (pidx, tidx) if valid_next else (pidx, nidx)`).

Verified manually with several cases (`select a.*, b.c from a, b`, `select a.* from a, b`, `select a.b[1] from foo`, JSON `->`/`->>` operators, plain identifier lists) — all now produce correct grouped output and correct reindented formatting. arguments.summary:
Fixed a regression in sqlparse/engine/grouping.py's group_period() function. The post() callback had its conditional branches swapped: when the token following a '.' punctuation was a valid extension target (wildcard '*', a Function, SquareBrackets, or String.Single/T.Name), the code was returning (pidx, tidx) — stopping the group at the period itself — instead of (pidx, nidx) — extending the group through the next token. The branches were exactly inverted:

Before:
    return (pidx, tidx) if valid_next else (pidx, nidx)
After:
    return (pidx, nidx) if valid_next else (pidx, tidx)

This bug caused constructs like `a.*` (and `a.func()`, `a.b[1]`, etc.) to be grouped incorrectly as an Identifier ending right after the dot, leaving the wildcard/name as a separate sibling token. That broke downstream grouping stages (group_identifier_list, group_aliased) and produced incorrect reindent/format output such as `select a.*, b.c from a, b` not reindenting properly, JSON operator grouping, and wildcard grouping — matching the reported regression affecting 'format reindent: identifier list', 'format json ops', 'grouping identifier wildcard', and ~17 other related checks.

Verified the fix manually (no tests/ directory present in this sandboxed checkout) with sqlparse.format/parse on: `select a.*, b.c from a, b`, `select a.* from a, b`, `select a.b[1] from foo`, `select a[1], b from foo`, JSON operators (`->`, `->>`), MATCH/AGAINST, and plain identifier lists (`select a, b, c from foo`) — all now produce correct grouped structures and correctly reindented output, matching expected upstream behavior.
